Workshop 6 · Sessions 19–21 · Thursday 19 November 2026

Which words mean the same? Word vectors and word2vec

A customer searches a café app for cold tea. The best match is iced tea, but to a computer that only compares spellings, cold and iced have nothing in common. Today you teach a computer that they mean nearly the same, by looking at the words around them. Then you use the same idea on shopping baskets to find similar products.

Open slides Notebooks and data Practice problems

By the end of this workshop you can

  • explain the idea behind word vectors: words used in the same places get similar vectors
  • build a word's vector from its neighbour counts, by hand and in Python, and compare two words with cosine similarity
  • explain word2vec's guessing game: real neighbour pairs, fake pairs, the dot product and the sigmoid
  • work out one nudge step of word2vec by hand, and say why it moves two vectors closer or further apart
  • train word2vec on 30,000 real reviews, learn product vectors from what customers reviewed, and say what word vectors get wrong: opposites and bias

Course outcome CO2 · Reading: [SLP] Chapter 5, sections 5.2, 5.5, 5.7 and 5.8

2. Where you already meet this

Word vectors sit behind many things that seem to understand what you mean:

  • a search box that finds iced tea when you typed cold tea
  • "you may also like" boxes in shops, music and travel apps, learned from what people buy, play or click
  • the keyboard on your phone suggesting words that fit, not just words that are spelled alike

3. The whole idea in five minutes

A word is known by its neighbours. iced and cold both come just before latte, tea and coffee. So describe each word by the words around it: count, for every word of the vocabulary, how often it is a neighbour. That list of counts is the word's vector, and cosine similarity compares two of them. iced and cold come out alike, even if they never appear in the same sentence.

Word2vec: a short list, learned by a guessing game. Counting gives one number per vocabulary word: 50,000 numbers for a real vocabulary, almost all 0. Word2vec gives every word a short list instead, say 100 numbers, and learns them by playing "is this a real neighbour pair, or a fake one?". Real pairs come from the text, fake pairs pair a word with a random word. The guess is

\[ \text{guess} = \sigma(w \cdot c) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-w \cdot c}} \]

where w · c is the dot product of the two lists and the sigmoid σ turns it into a chance between 0 and 1. After each guess, both lists are nudged: error = target − guess (target 1 for real, 0 for fake), and each list moves by rate × error × the other list. Words with the same neighbours are nudged the same way, so their vectors end up close.

Not just words. Treat each customer's list of products as a sentence and each product as a word, and products bought by the same customers get similar vectors.

4. Read

  • [SLP] Jurafsky & Martin, Chapter 5, Embeddings: section 5.2 (the intuition), 5.5 up to the end of 5.5.2 (word2vec: the classifier and how it learns), 5.7 (semantic properties, analogies) and 5.8 (bias). Skim the equations in 5.5.2; the lab writes the same step in plain Python.

5. Try (optional)

Open a shopping site and look at the "customers also bought" box under any product. Are the suggestions similar products, or products that go with it? Which of the two would a model trained on baskets give?

Handout: word vectors cheat sheet

Print this page, or keep it open during the lab.

Words

neighbour the word just before or just after
neighbour-count vector one count per vocabulary word: how often it is a neighbour
word vector a list of numbers for a word; words used alike get similar lists
real pair a word and a neighbour from the text
fake pair a word and a random word
sigmoid turns any score into a chance between 0 and 1
nudge a small change to both lists after a guess
rate how big each nudge is

Formulas

score w · c = w₁c₁ + w₂c₂ + …
sigmoid σ(x) = 1 ÷ (1 + e⁻ˣ)
guess σ(w · c)
error target − guess (target 1 real, 0 fake)
new w w + rate × error × c
new c c + rate × error × w (old w)
cosine w · c ÷ (|w| × |c|)
σ values σ(−2) 0.12 · σ(−1) 0.27 · σ(0) 0.50 · σ(1) 0.73 · σ(2) 0.88

Worked example: one nudge

Real pair (iced, latte). iced = [1, 0], latte = [0, 1], rate = 0.5.

Step Working Result
score 1×0 + 0×1 0
guess σ(0) 0.50
error 1 − 0.50 0.50
rate × error 0.5 × 0.50 0.25
new iced [1, 0] + 0.25 × [0, 1] [1, 0.25]
new latte [0, 1] + 0.25 × [1, 0] (the old iced) [0.25, 1]
new guess σ(1×0.25 + 0.25×1) = σ(0.5) 0.62

For a fake pair the target is 0, the error is negative, and the two lists move apart.

Python

pairs.append((w[i], w[i + 1])) add the pair (word, the word after)
counts[n] += 1 one more time n was a neighbour
1 / (1 + math.exp(-x)) the sigmoid
w[k] = old_w + rate * error * old_c nudge one number
random.choice(vocab) a random word, for a fake pair
nearest("iced", W) the words whose vectors are closest
